knowledge_type_note: Typed tablebase-fact rather than positional-concept because the core claim is provable and has been proved here: the same position is a draw or a win purely according to who must move. That is not a heuristic.

attributions.note: Credited with the formulation that the opposition is a means to an end, the end being penetration to a key square.

history.notes: No coinage researched. The technique is ancient and anonymous; Averbakh's corrective is the attributable part and is second-hand here.

engine_era_note: Fully settled by tablebase, and the proof is a one-bit comparison. Nothing about the concept has been revised; what tablebases add is that the exceptions — positions where taking the opposition is the wrong move — can now be demonstrated rather than argued.

preconditions: Both kings on the same rank or file with exactly one square between them
indicators_for: A king-and-pawn endgame where king penetration decides the result
The defending king is trying to hold key squares in front of a pawn
Neither side has a spare pawn tempo
indicators_against: A spare pawn tempo exists, so the opposition can be handed back
The position is decided by a race rather than by penetration
Taking the opposition does not lead to any key square — Averbakh's point
Enough material remains that king movement is not the deciding factor
false_positive_traps: Kings facing each other is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides.
Taking the opposition is not always correct. In some positions the king should ignore it and head for a key square directly — this is Averbakh's corrective and it is the standard error.
A spare pawn tempo makes the opposition irrelevant, since it can simply be handed back.

typical_plans: Take the opposition to force the defending king aside, then occupy a key square
Convert distant or diagonal opposition into direct opposition as an intermediate step
As the defender, seize the opposition whenever the attacking king advances
typical_moves: A king step that leaves exactly one square between the kings
A waiting king move on the same file
typical_piece_arrangements: Kings two squares apart on a file, pawn behind the attacking king
strategic_consequences: The reason a single tempo is worth so much in simplified positions

exceptions: Taking the opposition is not always best. Averbakh: it is a means to an end, and if it does not lead to a key square, marching the king there directly may be correct.
A spare pawn tempo neutralises it entirely.
In positions decided by a pawn race, king geometry may be irrelevant.
limitations: Mechanically detectable and mechanically decidable in the endgame; meaningless elsewhere.

Confined to endgames, per the record's own first trap that kings facing each other "is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides". 0.6% of the 788 shipped positions. It reports who HAS the opposition and cannot say whether taking it is right - the record's second trap, Averbakh's corrective, is a judgement about the plan.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the matcher's own `implements` string claimed the wording named the third trap - 'a spare pawn tempo makes the opposition irrelevant, since it can simply be handed back' - and the wording did not. It does now, and the claim drops to LOW confidence when the side to move has a pawn push that loses nothing, which is the commonest reason a king that 'has the opposition' has nothing.

MEASURED 2026-09-02: the trap 'taking the opposition is not always correct. In some positions the king should ignore it and head for a key square directly - this is Averbakh's correction' is a claim about which MOVE to play, and this matcher never recommends one: it reports which side holds the opposition, and now also when a spare pawn tempo hands it straight back. Whether taking it is right needs the key squares of the specific pawn ending, which this base does not compute and does not pretend to.
misconceptions: That having the opposition means it is your move. It means the opposite — the side NOT to move has it.
That taking the opposition is always right.
That it is a rule of thumb. In king-and-pawn endings it is provably exact.

examples.note: Constructed controlled pair, positive half. White Ke5, pawn e4, Black Ke7 — direct opposition. BLACK to move, so White has the opposition.

tablebase.note: PROVEN win for White, mate in 28. Result is from the side to move (Black). Paired with the identical position with White to move, which is a proven draw. The two FENs differ in exactly one character — the side-to-move field — which makes this the most tightly isolated controlled pair possible in chess.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN WIN for White, dtz -4, mate in 28 from Black's side, and the engine reports mate in 15 for the side not to move. Black to move must give ground. This single position serves `opposition`, `key-square` and `zugzwang` at once, and the pair it belongs to - the same board with White to move, proven DRAWN - is the strictest controlled comparison this base contains, because nothing on the board differs at all.

counterexamples.note: CORRECTED 2026-09-02. The counterexample here used to be the SAME board as the positive with only the side to move changed, labelled negative - and that was wrong: the opposition is present in both halves, held by whoever is NOT to move, so this base reports it in both and was being marked down for being right. The concept is per-side and the old entry read it as per-position. What replaces it is a real negative: the same two kings one square apart with a rook each still on the board, which is this record's own first trap - 'kings facing each other is trivially detectable and MEANS NOTHING outside endgames where king penetration decides'. The matcher's endgame gate refuses it, and the tablebase says why it should: with rooks on, the position is decided by Rh8+ and a mating net rather than by whose turn it is.

tablebase.note: PROVEN WIN in 21, best move Rh8+. The kings stand in opposition and it decides nothing: the rooks decide it. That is the record's first trap stated as a proven result rather than as an opinion.

That is this record's first trap - kings facing each other means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides - stated as a proven result rather than as an opinion.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `opposition-pattern-without-condition`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Kings facing each other with one square between them on a rank or file. The side NOT to move has the opposition. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Kings facing each other is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

The negative half of the strictest pair in this base: the same board as the winning position with only the side to move changed. Whoever is NOT to move holds the opposition, which is why this half of the pair is a negative for three concepts and not a different position.

by_level.beginner: The two kings are facing each other with one square between. Whoever has to move must step aside, so you want it to be their turn, not yours.
by_level.intermediate: Direct opposition. The side NOT to move has it. Use it to force their king off the squares in front of your pawn.
by_level.advanced: Opposition, a special case of zugzwang. Remember Averbakh: it is a means to an end, and the end is a key square — sometimes marching there directly beats taking it.
by_level.master: Decidable. In king-and-pawn endings the opposition is exact, and the corresponding-squares framework generalises it for cluttered positions where simple opposition misleads.

by_depth.short: Kings face each other; whoever must move gives way.
by_depth.normal: The opposition: kings on the same line with one square between them. Because kings cannot touch, whoever is to move has to step aside — so the side NOT to move has the opposition and can force the other king off key squares.
by_depth.deep: A special case of zugzwang, and one of the few chess ideas that is exactly provable. In the basic king-and-pawn-versus-king position the same arrangement is a draw with one side to move and a win in 28 with the other — a full point turning on a single bit. Diagonal and distant opposition are variants, usually used as routes to the direct form. The corrective that matters is Averbakh's: the opposition is a means to an end and the end is penetration to a key square. Taking it is not automatically correct, and in some positions the king should simply march for the key squares instead.

explanations.lesson: In king-and-pawn endings, work out who has the opposition before you move — and then check that taking it actually gets your king somewhere it wants to be.

beginner_words: whoever moves has to give way
avoid: I have the opposition because it is my move

definition_short: Kings facing each other with one square between them on a rank or file. The side NOT to move has the opposition.
definition_long:
Two kings a knight's-jump-less apart — one empty square between them on a rank or file. Since kings may not stand adjacent, each blocks the other, and whoever must move has to give way. The player NOT on move is said to have the opposition.

It is a special case of zugzwang, and its effect is exact rather than approximate. In the basic king-and-pawn-versus-king position with White Ke5, pawn e4, Black Ke7, the tablebase gives a DRAW with White to move and a WIN for White (mate in 28) with Black to move. Same pieces, same squares; one bit of difference.

Variants: DIAGONAL opposition, kings on a diagonal with one square between; DISTANT opposition, kings on the same line with an odd number of squares between, where again the player not to move holds it. Both are usually routes to direct opposition.

AVERBAKH'S CORRECTIVE is the part most often missed: the opposition is a MEANS TO AN END, and the end is penetration to a KEY SQUARE. Taking the opposition is not automatically right. Wikipedia's own example makes the point — in one position 1.Ke2 taking the distant opposition wins, while in another taking the opposition with 1.Ke4 only draws and the king should simply march for the key squares instead.
